name: Refugee/Asylum Status

requirements.blocker_text: Malaysia is not a signatory to the 1951 Refugee Convention, its 1967 Protocol, the 1954 Convention on Statelessness, or the 1961 Convention on the Reduction of Statelessness, and has no comprehensive domestic legal or policy framework to identify or protect asylum-seekers or refugees. Malaysian law does not distinguish asylum-seekers or refugees from undocumented migrants, leaving them formally exposed to the same arrest, detention, and deportation provisions under the Immigration Act. UNHCR is permitted to register, conduct refugee status determination, and provide assistance in Malaysia, but this UNHCR-issued documentation is not a Malaysian government-recognised legal status and does not itself authorise residence or work.

sources.title: Forced Migration Review (a UNHCR-affiliated academic publication) -- 'Refugees and space in urban areas in Malaysia,' confirming Malaysia's non-signatory status to the 1951 Convention, its 1967 Protocol, and both statelessness conventions

UNHCR submission to Malaysia's Universal Periodic Review -- confirming the 2005 Attorney General's Circular providing limited prosecutorial immunity for UNHCR-registered asylum-seekers and refugees, and the absence of a comprehensive domestic legal framework

notes: Uses the same 'never existed, not closed' convention established for the UAE, Saudi Arabia, and Singapore elsewhere in this dataset (closed_date: null, superseded_by: null), since there is no prior formal asylum system that was abolished -- one never existed to begin with. Malaysia joins this group as a fourth confirmed case in this build, reinforcing that the pattern spans multiple regions (Gulf states and maritime Southeast Asia) rather than being geographically confined. A genuine partial nuance distinguishes Malaysia's case from a completely blank slate, however, and is worth stating precisely rather than flattened into an identical 'nothing exists' description: a 2005 Attorney General's Circular provides UNHCR-registered asylum-seekers and refugees a degree of immunity from prosecution under the Immigration Act specifically -- a real, if narrow and purely administrative-discretion-based, accommodation that stops short of any codified legal status, work authorisation, or right to residence. This is analogous in shape (an informal accommodation layered on top of a 'never existed' formal system) to the discretionary humanitarian practices noted for Saudi Arabia elsewhere in this dataset, and is precisely why this route is modeled hard:false rather than omitted entirely -- the honest content here is the notice of this partial accommodation and its formal limits, not a disqualifying test. Malaysia hosts a substantial population under this arrangement -- UNHCR figures cited in sources checked for this build put registered and unregistered asylum-seekers, refugees, and stateless persons in the range of 100,000+ (predominantly Rohingya and other Myanmar nationals) -- making this a materially significant gap in Malaysia's formal immigration-route landscape despite the country's engagement with UNHCR on registration and status determination. The Malaysian Federal Constitution separately provides a narrow statelessness-prevention mechanism (a child born in Malaysia who cannot acquire any other country's nationality is a Malaysian citizen) -- not modeled as its own route here since it addresses statelessness specifically rather than functioning as an asylum or refugee-protection mechanism, but flagged as a related constitutional safeguard worth noting alongside this route.
